rounds.what: The round's own observation from round 8 became code: an option-shaped stem is refused. Two texts the change had made false were corrected, and the class search behind them was re-derived and its fourth hit confirmed against the repository's own standard for marking a retired section.

implementerProof.how: Round 9: I drove the dash refusal and its discrimination rather than reading the rule, ran both halves of the suite and found the comparison weaker than its count suggests, checked both corrected texts against the mechanism and one of them against the helper it cites, and confirmed the class search's fourth hit against INFRA-212's standard by measuring the distances rather than accepting that the marker exists. Where I could not identify a line its handoff named, I asked rather than guessed, and the implementer corrected its own wording in the answer. Rounds 1 to 8 were each verified as those rounds record.

proof.criterion: A directory name that looks like a command option is refused, without refusing the names actually in use.
proof.surface: The real `session_copy` at this head, and the 51-case suite run at this head and against the script as it was at the previous head.
proof.command: Drive stems `-rf`, `-`, `--`, `-n`, `--force`, then `a-b`, `legion-infra-infra-80`, `_x`, `.hidden`; then `bun test scripts/e2e/lib/stage4b-session-text.test.ts` here and against `jj file show -r 00516adc6b34`'s script
proof.observed: Every option-shaped stem is refused by name with nothing written; every plain name is accepted and copied, including the real pod-name shape, which contains `-` in a non-leading position — a blunt rule would have refused every stem in use. The suite is 51 pass / 0 fail here and 43 pass / 8 fail against the previous head's script.
proof.negativeControl: The accepted row is the control on the refusal: `legion-infra-infra-80` and `a-b` are copied normally, so the refusals are the leading-dash rule firing and not the function failing.
proof.doesNotSettle: The eight-against-forty-three is a true count and a weaker claim than it looks: only one of the eight is a behaviour difference. The other seven — `..`, `.`, empty, a `/`, a `/` that climbs, a byte outside the class, and a stem from a session file ending `/..` — fail because the refusal's wording changed; I drove those same shapes against that same script in round 8 and each was already refused with nothing written. The implementer's own negative control says 'that one case', which agrees. The leading-dash case is the evidence; the count is not.

proof.criterion: The two texts this change had made false are now true of the mechanism.
proof.surface: The manual's node-packing paragraph against the two pod kinds' volume sources, and the issue-independence comment against the helper it names.
proof.command: Read the paragraph against `issuePod.diskSource` and `controllerPod.diskSource`; read the comment against `pod_disk` in the same script
proof.observed: The node-packing distinction holds: the controller's pod mounts the claim its Sandbox owns, so a relaunch onto another node waits for a `ReadWriteOnce` detach and shows `FailedAttachVolume`/`Multi-Attach`; an issue pod mounts a generic ephemeral claim created with it, takes no predecessor's claim, and waits on nothing detaching. What it may wait on — the predecessor's claim being reaped — is the mechanism I measured on a real cluster in round 1, about a second after the pod was deleted. The issue-independence comment agrees with `pod_disk`, which runs `op get pvc "$1-issue" --ignore-not-found` and reports the claim's name, phase and controller owner, with no label selector anywhere in it.
proof.negativeControl: The paragraph is a distinction rather than a deletion: the controller half must stay true, and it does — its Sandbox still owns its claim (`controllerPod.claimTemplates`), so the detach wait it describes is still that pod's behaviour.

proof.criterion: The class search's fourth hit is correct, and its retirement is marked where a reader meets it.
proof.surface: `docs/kubernetes.md` at this head, measured against the standard `docs/solutions/legion/…-INFRA-212.md` sets.
proof.command: Locate the sentence, the nearest heading above it and the marker; count the file's markers of that shape; count what points into the heading by anchor
proof.observed: The hit is `:4853` — a tree's pods required onto one node by `podAffinity` because the tree's volume is one `ReadWriteOnce` PVC — false of this release in every clause and true of the subsection's. My own class search missed it because it keyed on `detach` and `outlives` where this reaches by `ReadWriteOnce`. INFRA-212 requires the retirement marked where a reader enters, who 'reads upward only to the nearest `###`': the sentence is at `:4853`, the heading `### Anatomy of a pod` at `:4840`, and the marker at `:4842` — two lines under the heading, eleven above the sentence. A reader who looks up meets it. Twelve markers of that shape are in the file.
proof.negativeControl: The measurement is the control: had the marker been under the `##` rather than the `###`, a reader reading upward to the nearest heading would never reach it, which is the defect INFRA-212 was filed for. The distances are what decide it, not the marker's existence.
proof.doesNotSettle: A reader who looks up not at all is unreached, which is true of all twelve markers. The stronger fix — the word in the heading — is counter-indicated by INFRA-212's own cost analysis, except for this heading: `](#anatomy-of-a-pod)` is referenced nowhere in the repository outside the learning that names it, so this is the cheap case. An option for the reviewer rather than a finding.
